headline: Tech stocks took a hit last night with Microsoft and Google both down around 4%, while the ASX held steady and oil surged on Middle East tensions — keep an eye on your US holdings tonight.

portfolio.summary: The big story is in your US tech holdings — Microsoft and Google both fell hard last night, dragging on the overall feel of your portfolio even though your ASX positions barely moved. Emerging markets (VGE) was a quiet bright spot on the local market today.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft fell $19 last night to $441. The drop likely reflects broader tech sector jitters and profit-taking after a strong run. Morningstar has a $600 fair value target and Morgan Stanley is bullish on AI revenue, so the long-term case remains intact — but it stung last night.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google dropped nearly $15 last night to $361. No specific breaking news drove this — it moved with the broader tech selloff. There's ongoing noise about AI competition but analysts are still broadly positive on the stock.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two slipped just over 2% last night to $222. GTA 6 remains locked in for a November release (Take-Two has officially filed that date), which removes delay risk — but the market mood weighed on it regardless.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: A quiet winner in today's ASX session, up 0.7% to $93.65. Emerging markets have been benefiting from a steady Aussie dollar and improving sentiment toward Asia.

movers.name: BetaShares Global Energy ETF
movers.note: Nudged up 0.35% today, consistent with oil prices rising last night on Iran-US tensions and Middle East conflict. More on that in the watch section.

movers.name: Commonwealth Bank
movers.note: Barely moved today, down just 18 cents to $163. RBA interest rate concerns are keeping a lid on bank stocks, but nothing dramatic here.

markets.summary: Last night's US session was a mixed bag — the big indices (S&P 500 and NASDAQ) were basically flat, but under the hood, tech got whacked while oil and gold pushed higher. The ASX 200 data for today's close didn't come through properly, but your ASX holdings suggest a calm day locally. The Aussie dollar is holding steady around 71.8 US cents.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Essentially flat last night — the index held up despite weakness in big tech names.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Near-zero move last night despite MSFT and GOOGL falling — other sectors offset the tech drag.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil jumped $1.43 last night amid Iran-US strikes and the Israel-Lebanon conflict keeping supply fears alive.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold continues its strong run, up nearly 1% last night. Safe-haven demand from geopolitical tensions is keeping the price elevated.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar is barely changed, hovering just above 71.8 US cents.

politics.summary: The RBA is dominating the domestic news today, with debate heating up over whether high interest rates are starting to hurt property prices — and whether the Reserve Bank will ease off. RBA board member Ian Harper flagged that inflation is still sticking around, signalling rate cuts aren't coming as fast as many hoped.

stories.title: RBA and Treasurer Chalmers clash over what's driving house price falls
stories.why_it_matters: Both the RBA and Treasurer Jim Chalmers are pointing fingers at high interest rates and the tax system for a softening in house prices. This is politically sensitive — falling house prices hurt existing owners but help first-home buyers. The debate signals the government is watching the property market closely, and any further falls could add pressure on the RBA to start cutting rates sooner.

stories.title: RBA's Harper warns inflation persistence is still a 'significant issue'
stories.why_it_matters: RBA board member Ian Harper said today that inflation is still proving stubborn — meaning the Reserve Bank isn't ready to cut rates just yet. For mortgage holders hoping for relief, this is a cold shower. For your CBA holding, steady rates can support bank margins short-term, but prolonged high rates also increase the risk of loan defaults down the track.

stories.title: News.com.au: 'Bitter RBA blow for Australian households'
stories.why_it_matters: This piece reflects growing public frustration with the RBA keeping rates high while household budgets are being squeezed. Everyday Aussies are feeling the pinch on mortgages and cost of living simultaneously. If rates stay elevated into the second half of 2026, consumer spending will continue to slow — which flows through to the broader economy and could weigh on ASX-listed retailers and banks.

ai.summary: AI regulation is the big theme today — Trump signed an executive order giving the US government early access to new AI models, and there's a fascinating internal war within the Trump administration over how (or whether) to regulate AI at all. Separately, a new study found that every major AI company — OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Amazon and xAI — fails against a specific type of attack.

stories.title: Trump signs executive order for early access to new AI releases
stories.why_it_matters: Trump signed an executive order today requiring AI companies to submit their most advanced models to the US government for review before wide release, with a focus on cybersecurity. This gives the government an early look at cutting-edge AI — think of it like a regulatory test-drive before the public gets access. For companies like Google and Microsoft, this means more government scrutiny on new products, which could slow some releases but also creates a formal channel for government AI adoption.

stories.title: Trump White House is at war with itself over AI regulation
stories.why_it_matters: WIRED reports the Trump administration is deeply divided on AI — some officials want to regulate it heavily for national security reasons, while others want to keep government hands off to let US companies race ahead of China. This internal tension means US AI policy could swing dramatically in either direction. For investors, regulatory uncertainty is the enemy of steady returns in the AI sector.

stories.title: All major AI companies fail the same type of security attack, study finds
stories.why_it_matters: A new study found that OpenAI (ChatGPT), Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), Amazon (Bedrock) and Elon Musk's xAI all fail against a specific category of attack — the study doesn't specify which type, but the key point is that no single company has solved this vulnerability. For Google and Microsoft investors, it's a reminder that AI safety is still a work in progress and could attract more regulation or reputational risk if these gaps are exploited publicly.

stories.title: Microsoft and Google are 'absolutely critical' competitors in AI coding — but they're late
stories.why_it_matters: CNBC analysts say Microsoft and Google are essential competitors in the booming AI coding tools market — where developers pay for AI to help write software — but both are playing catch-up to specialist tools like GitHub Copilot rivals and startups. The AI coding market is worth tens of billions of dollars, and analysts say it's 'absolutely critical' for both companies' future growth. A positive long-term signal for MSFT and GOOGL, even if the road is bumpy right now.

sport.summary: NRL Round 14 is the big local story — team lists are out, the Broncos have dropped a selection bombshell, and there's big signing news across the competition. The Warriors are on a bye this week. AFL also got a mention with some interesting form analysis.

stories.title: Broncos axe Origin gun from Round 14 squad; Bulldogs make big Crichton call
stories.why_it_matters: Brisbane Broncos coach Michael Maguire (Madge) has axed an Origin representative from the Round 14 squad — a bold call with State of Origin season in full swing. The Bulldogs are also making a big decision around Matt Crichton. This reshuffling could affect the Broncos vs Titans clash at Suncorp on Saturday night, which is the marquee Queensland derby of the round.

stories.title: Kel Foran named Manly Sea Eagles head coach; Origin rep signs with two clubs in one day
stories.why_it_matters: Kel Foran has been confirmed as Manly Sea Eagles head coach — a significant appointment for a club that's been through coaching turmoil. Separately, an Origin representative managed to officially sign with two clubs in the same day (reportedly a paperwork timing situation), creating an unusual contractual saga that the NRL will need to sort out.

stories.title: PNG land fourth signing; Origin star locks in move to the Chiefs (rugby union)
stories.why_it_matters: The Papua New Guinea Hunters have locked in their fourth NRL-level signing as the PNG franchise builds toward its entry into the competition. Elsewhere, an Origin star has confirmed a switch to the Chiefs rugby union team — another high-profile cross-code move that highlights the growing competition for elite Queensland talent.

stories.title: AFL: Daylight splitting the top tier from the rest — NFL-style 'superteam' nightmare is alive
stories.why_it_matters: Fox Sports analysis argues a massive gap is forming between the AFL's elite clubs and the pack — similar to the 'superteam' problem that has plagued the NFL. The data shows the top few teams are pulling away in form, percentage, and talent, raising questions about competition balance for the second half of the 2026 season.

watch_today.title: MSFT & GOOGL: Sharp falls last night — hold steady
watch_today.detail: Microsoft dropped 4.2% and Google fell 3.9% last night in what looks like a broad tech selloff rather than company-specific bad news. The long-term analyst thesis is intact — Morningstar has MSFT at fair value of $600 and Morgan Stanley is positive on AI revenue. No reason to sell into this dip, but worth watching tonight's US open to see if the selling continues.

watch_today.title: GOOGL: Hold through the dip — AI competition is the real long-term watch
watch_today.detail: Google is down nearly 4% from last night's close. The CNBC story today flagged that Google is 'absolutely critical' in AI coding but playing catch-up. No specific negative catalyst from Google's own operations — this feels like market noise. Hold and watch.

watch_today.title: Oil surging on Middle East tensions — FUEL.AX is a beneficiary
watch_today.detail: WTI crude oil jumped 1.55% last night to US$93.59, driven by Iran-US strikes and the Israel-Lebanon conflict. Your FUEL.AX (global energy ETF) nudged up 0.35% today in response. If tensions escalate further, oil could push higher and lift this holding more meaningfully. No need to act — just a nice tailwind to be aware of.

watch_today.title: GTA 6 locked in for November — TTWO catalyst ahead
watch_today.detail: Take-Two has officially filed paperwork locking GTA 6 to a November 2026 release. This removes the biggest risk that's hung over the stock — another delay. As the release date gets closer, expect more marketing hype and potentially a stock re-rating. The -2% last night was market noise, not GTA news. Hold heading into what should be a big few months.

watch_today.title: RBA rate cut hopes fading — watch impact on AUD and your US holdings
watch_today.detail: RBA board member Ian Harper said today that inflation is still too sticky to cut rates soon. This keeps the Aussie dollar supported (currently 71.8 US cents), which slightly reduces the AUD value of your US-denominated holdings (GOOGL, MSFT, TTWO) when you eventually convert back. Not an immediate concern, but something to factor in if you're thinking about rebalancing.
